opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because those two kinds of testing actually look quite different in practice, even though we bring them together in the same evaluation experience.

On the quality side, you're asking things like: is the response grounded in the source data I gave it? Is it relevant to the user's question? Is it coherent and fluent? Those are things you want to measure on your typical, expected traffic. You build a dataset that represents how your users are actually going to use the application, you run it through, and you get a picture of how well the system is doing its job. That's something you do continuously, every time you change a prompt or swap out a model.

Responsible AI risks are different, because the failures you care about usually don't show up in normal usage. If you just test on your everyday traffic, you might never see the model produce hateful content, or help with self-harm, or leak something through a jailbreak, but that doesn't mean it can't. So for those, you have to go looking for the problem. It's adversarial testing. You need to deliberately probe the system the way a bad actor, or just a user in a vulnerable moment, might.

That's where the challenge comes in for most customers: they don't have a big red team, and they don't have adversarial datasets sitting around for every risk category. So one of the things we did was build on the red teaming expertise we have at Microsoft and essentially automate it. We use an adversarial simulator that can play the role of a user trying to elicit harmful content, have multi-turn conversations with your application, try jailbreak techniques, and so on. Then we use AI-assisted evaluators, essentially our safety classifiers and LLM-based judges that we've calibrated carefully against human labels, to score those conversations for things like violence, sexual content, self-harm, hate and unfairness, and susceptibility to jailbreaks.

So the short version is: for quality, you bring your representative data and we help you measure it. For risk, we help you generate the hard data you probably don't have, and then measure it. Then you look at both together, because the real goal is to make trade-offs. Often a mitigation that makes the system safer could affect quality, or vice versa, and you want to see that in one place, iterate, and make an informed decision before you ship, and then keep monitoring in production.

r001.rationale: The response says quality evaluation uses a dataset representing how users will actually use the application.

r002.rationale: It says customers often lack adversarial datasets for every risk category.

r003.rationale: It describes using an adversarial simulator to generate multi-turn conversations that probe for harmful content and jailbreaks.

r004.rationale: It mentions AI-assisted evaluators calibrated against human labels, but does not describe converting hateful-content guidelines written for expert human linguists into a GPT-4 prompt.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because they really are two different problems, even though they live in the same evaluation toolkit.

With quality metrics, things like groundedness, relevance, coherence, you're mostly evaluating against the data you expect to see. You take a representative sample of what your users are actually going to send to the application, you run it through, and you measure how well the system is doing. The goal is to understand typical behavior. And honestly, if your application is slightly less relevant on some edge case, that's a quality issue, it's not a catastrophe.

Responsible AI risks are the opposite. If you only test with your expected traffic, you'll almost never see the problems, because the problems happen in the tails. They happen when someone is deliberately trying to get the system to produce hateful content, or leak something it shouldn't, or when a jailbreak is embedded in a document the model retrieves. So for those, you can't rely on your normal data. You have to go generate the adversarial cases on purpose.

That's why we built the adversarial simulator into the evaluation flow. It uses a model, with the safety guardrails intentionally relaxed for this purpose, to play the role of an attacker and have a multi-turn conversation with your application, probing for specific harm categories, hate and unfairness, sexual content, violence, self-harm, and also things like jailbreak susceptibility and protected material. You get coverage of scenarios your real users haven't sent you yet, and hopefully never will, but that a motivated bad actor absolutely would.

The other difference is in how you score and interpret the results. For quality, an aggregate score is often what you want. For safety, the aggregate can be misleading. If 99.5 percent of responses are fine but half a percent are producing severe self-harm content, that half percent is the whole story. So we report severity levels, we surface the individual failing examples, and we really push people to go read them rather than just look at a number on a dashboard.

And then the last piece is that these two things interact. When you add a mitigation for a safety risk, say a stricter content filter or a system prompt change, you very often take a hit on quality, you get more refusals, more over-blocking. So in practice we tell people to run both sets of evaluations together, every time they make a change, so they can actually see the tradeoff they're making rather than discovering it in production.

r001.rationale: It says to use a representative sample of what users will send to the application to evaluate quality metrics.

r002.rationale: It explains that normal or expected-traffic data will almost never reveal tail risks, so builders cannot rely on their usual data to exercise those risks.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says to generate adversarial cases on purpose and describes a simulator probing the application for harm categories.

r004.rationale: It does not describe translating expert linguists’ hateful-content scoring guidelines into a GPT-4 prompt for automated scoring.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you’re testing for different things. With quality metrics, you want to understand how well the system performs on the tasks people will actually use it for. So you need a representative set of examples: the questions users are likely to ask, the kinds of documents they’ll bring, and what a good response looks like.

With Responsible AI risks, representative usage alone isn’t enough. A harmful response might be very rare, but still be something you really need to address. So you deliberately test the boundaries. You ask questions that could elicit harmful content, try adversarial inputs, and explore situations where the safeguards might fail.

Those evaluations complement each other. You want to know both, ‘Does my application work well for its intended purpose?’ and, ‘What happens when it encounters a difficult or potentially harmful situation?’ And you want to repeat both kinds of testing as you change the model, the prompt, or the safeguards, because improving one dimension can affect another.

r001.rationale: It calls for examples representative of what users will ask and the documents they will bring, matching the application's production data.

r002.rationale: It says representative usage alone is insufficient, but does not state that application builders often lack datasets that exercise Responsible AI risks.

r003.rationale: It describes deliberately asking questions that could elicit harmful content and trying adversarial inputs to test Responsible AI risks.

r004.rationale: It does not mention hateful-content scoring guidelines, expert human linguists, or converting guidelines into a GPT-4 prompt.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about those as two complementary layers. On the quality side, you’re asking, “Is this application doing its job?” Is the answer relevant? Is it grounded in the information you provided? Those are things you want to measure on examples that represent how people will actually use the system.

With Responsible AI risks, you also need to ask, “What happens when things go wrong?” Your typical usage data may not contain the cases that expose a serious safety issue. So you need targeted tests and adversarial testing—deliberately probing for harmful responses and looking at how the application behaves under pressure.

The evaluation tools help you do both systematically. But the tests and the thresholds need to reflect your application and its context. You want to evaluate the whole system, including the safeguards you’ve put in place, and repeat those evaluations as you make changes. A quality improvement doesn’t automatically mean a safety improvement, so you need visibility into both.

r001.rationale: It says quality should be measured on examples representative of how people will actually use the system.

r002.rationale: It observes that typical usage data may not contain cases that expose serious safety issues.

r003.rationale: It calls for targeted and adversarial tests that deliberately probe for harmful responses.

r004.rationale: It does not mention hateful-content guidelines, expert human linguists, or adapting them into a GPT-4 prompt for automated scoring.
